Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

DOHA, Qatar (CNN) -- If there's anything in which Qatar takes pride -- aside from a massive construction boom -- it is providing its Qatari minority and the hundreds of thousands of expatriates working and living here with plenty of shopping opportunities. City Center Mall booked "Freestyle Football" artist Iya Traore, from Guinea, to help draw more crowds in Doha . You can nary drive a kilometer in Doha -- few Qataris actually walk the streets -- without passing a shopping mall. And few of those malls are lacking hordes of people strolling from store to store. From the pricey jewel-adorned head scarf fashions to budget-conscious it-could-be-rat-leather shoes, food courts to suit Eastern and Western tastes, to perfume shops selling essences for more per ounce than many people earn in a month -- shoppers in Doha are spoiled for choice. I'm lucky to have a few Qatari national friends in Doha. Each time I visit, I'm treated to a familiar, and always entertaining, routine ... passing time at a succession of shopping centers. Yes, many of you may think this pastime -- especially in America -- is for the kiddies. You are right. And yes, my friends and I are in our 30s. But there's a more sophisticated, Arab cultural aspect to "hanging out" at a Starbucks at Landmark Shopping Center or drinking mint tea at one of the restaurants in the renovated Souq Waqif. For many "shoppers" -- male and female -- these centers are an opportunity catch up with friends, and discretely flirt and mingle ... even if only by exchanging messages via Bluetooth on the cellphone. And unlike many teenyboppers cruising the malls of America, most of the adults here are a shop owner's dream: high-end, impulse purchasing consumers with a lot of money to spend -- and a lot of time to kill. Little surprise then, that shopping mall developers and management have taken to providing more entertainment options to pull in the crowds: The obligatory movie theater, for example. One mall's basement is host to a skating rink. At a recent stop at City Center-Doha Mall, thumping hip-hop beats had kids dropping their McDonald's ice cream cones and running to the center atrium to see what all the fuss was about. Turns out there's this athlete literally center stage of the mall, kicking and balancing a soccer ball -- OK, football -- about his head, shoulders, legs and back with such skill he might put Ronaldo to shame -- and doing this to the beat of hip-hop African tunes for what seemed more than just a few minutes. Guinean native Iya Traore's "freestyle soccer" routine mesmerized the crowd. Ironically, it distracted them from shopping -- but kept shoppers in the Mall longer and gave people something new to talk about. Apparently his athletic tricks have landed him television and live performances in Japan, Turkey, Mali, Germany, France and, increasingly, in the Arab world. Africa would seem a long way to book an act to attract more shoppers. But then again, the stakes are high in an increasingly competitive shopping mall-packed Qatar. As long as the mall remains an outlet to spend petro-dollars -- and Doha's main, all-access social networking scene -- mall developers will have to step up their game to keep consumers happy. E-mail to a friend .

outputs.L1:
**DOHA, Qatar (CNN) —** If there is anything in which Qatar takes pride—aside from its massive construction boom—it is providing the Qatari minority and the hundreds of thousands of expatriates who work and live here with abundant shopping opportunities.

City Center Mall booked Guinean “freestyle football” artist Iya Traore to help attract larger crowds in Doha.

You can scarcely drive a kilometer through Doha—few Qataris actually walk the streets—without passing a shopping mall. And few of those malls lack hordes of people strolling from store to store.

From pricey, jewel-adorned head-scarf fashions to budget-conscious shoes that could be made of rat leather; from food courts catering to Eastern and Western tastes to perfume shops selling essences that cost more per ounce than many people earn in a month—shoppers in Doha are spoiled for choice.

I am fortunate to have a few Qatari friends in Doha. Each time I visit, I am treated to a familiar and invariably entertaining routine: passing the time at a succession of shopping centers.

Yes, many of you—especially those in America—may think this pastime is for children. You are right. And yes, my friends and I are in our 30s.

But there is a more sophisticated, Arab cultural dimension to “hanging out” at a Starbucks in Landmark Shopping Center or drinking mint tea at one of the restaurants in the renovated Souq Waqif.

For many “shoppers,” both male and female, these centers offer an opportunity to catch up with friends and discreetly flirt and mingle—even if only by exchanging messages via Bluetooth on their cellphones.

And unlike many teenyboppers cruising America’s malls, most adults here are a shop owner’s dream: affluent, impulse-buying consumers with plenty of money to spend—and plenty of time to kill.

It is little surprise, then, that shopping mall developers and managers have begun providing more entertainment options to draw crowds. There is the obligatory movie theater, for example, while the basement of one mall houses a skating rink.

During a recent visit to City Center-Doha Mall, thumping hip-hop beats prompted children to drop their McDonald’s ice cream cones and run to the central atrium to see what all the commotion was about.

There, literally center stage in the mall, was an athlete kicking and balancing a soccer ball—OK, a football—on his head, shoulders, legs and back with such skill that he might put Ronaldo to shame. He performed to the rhythm of African hip-hop music for what seemed like far more than a few minutes.

Guinean native Iya Traore’s “freestyle soccer” routine mesmerized the crowd. Ironically, it distracted people from shopping—but it also kept shoppers in the mall longer and gave them something new to discuss.

His athletic tricks have apparently earned him television appearances and live performances in Japan, Turkey, Mali, Germany and France, as well as an increasing number of engagements in the Arab world.

Africa may seem a long way to go to book an act intended to attract more shoppers. Then again, the stakes are high in Qatar, where an already crowded shopping mall market is becoming increasingly competitive.

As long as the mall remains both an outlet for spending petro-dollars and Doha’s primary, all-access social-networking scene, mall developers will have to step up their game to keep consumers happy.

**E-mail to a friend.**

DOHA, Qatar (CNN) — Beyond its enormous building boom, Qatar is especially proud of the abundance of retail options available to both its relatively small Qatari population and the hundreds of thousands of foreign residents who live and work in the country.

To attract additional visitors in Doha, City Center Mall hired Iya Traore, a freestyle football performer from Guinea.

It is almost impossible to drive a kilometer through Doha without encountering a mall—walking is uncommon among Qataris—and most shopping centers are packed with people moving between stores. Doha offers consumers an extraordinary range of choices: expensive head scarves decorated with jewels, cheap shoes that look as though they could be made from rat leather, food courts serving both Eastern and Western cuisine, and fragrances priced per ounce at more than many workers earn in an entire month.

I am fortunate to have several Qatari friends in Doha. Whenever I visit, we follow the same enjoyable ritual: spending our free time moving from one mall to another.

Many readers, particularly Americans, may associate hanging around shopping centers with teenagers. That is fair enough, even though my friends and I are all in our 30s. In Qatar, however, the activity has a more refined cultural dimension. People gather over coffee at the Starbucks in Landmark Shopping Center or sip mint tea in restaurants at the restored Souq Waqif.

For many men and women described as “shoppers,” malls are really places to reconnect with friends and to flirt or socialize discreetly—even if that consists only of exchanging cellphone messages through Bluetooth. Unlike many young American mall-goers, most adult visitors in Qatar are ideal customers for retailers: affluent, spontaneous buyers with plenty of disposable income and ample time to fill.

Unsurprisingly, mall owners and managers have introduced additional attractions to increase foot traffic. Cinemas are now virtually standard, for instance, while the basement of one shopping center contains an ice-skating rink.

During a recent visit to City Center-Doha Mall, pounding hip-hop music prompted children to drop their McDonald’s ice-cream cones and rush toward the central atrium to discover what was happening. In the middle of the mall, an athlete was controlling and balancing a soccer ball—or football—with remarkable skill, moving it across his head, shoulders, legs and back. His ability might have embarrassed Ronaldo. He continued the routine, synchronized with African hip-hop tracks, for what felt like considerably longer than a few minutes.

The audience was captivated by Guinean-born Iya Traore’s freestyle football performance. Paradoxically, the show diverted attention away from shopping, yet it also encouraged visitors to stay inside the mall longer and gave them a fresh topic of conversation.

Traore’s athletic displays have reportedly earned him television appearances and live engagements in Japan, Turkey, Mali, Germany and France, as well as a growing number of performances across the Arab world.

Hiring an entertainer from Africa may appear an extreme measure simply to bring in more customers. Yet competition is intense in Qatar, where malls are increasingly numerous and the financial rewards are substantial.

As long as shopping centers remain both a place to spend oil wealth and Doha’s primary, widely accessible social network, developers will need to keep improving their offerings to satisfy consumers.

E-mail this story to a friend.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style travel and culture article about shopping malls as major social hubs in Doha, Qatar, highlighting expatriates, consumer culture, and a freestyle football performance by Guinea’s Iya Traore at City Center Mall.
counterfactuals.output:
# In Doha, the shopping mall is more than a place to buy

**Doha, Qatar** — Beneath the bright lights of City Center Mall, a football seemed to defy gravity.

Guinean freestyle footballer Iya Traore balanced the ball on his head, rolled it across his shoulders and flicked it skyward before catching it with the precision of a circus performer. Shoppers gathered around, phones raised. Children edged closer while families, office workers and tourists paused between restaurants and retail stores to watch.

The performance offered a snapshot of life in Doha, where shopping malls are not simply commercial spaces. In a city shaped by intense summer heat and a population drawn from around the world, they serve as climate-controlled town squares — places to meet, eat, exercise, celebrate and be entertained.

Traore, known for combining football skills with acrobatics, was a natural fit. Qatar’s passion for the sport intensified in the years surrounding the 2022 FIFA World Cup, but football had long been a shared language among the country’s diverse communities. At City Center, his routine transformed a retail concourse into a temporary arena.

## Doha’s indoor public squares

For much of the year, temperatures in Doha make extended outdoor activity difficult, particularly during the day. Malls provide a practical alternative: vast, air-conditioned environments where visitors can spend hours without needing a fixed plan.

City Center Mall, in the West Bay business district, sits among glass towers, hotels and offices. Its mix of international brands, supermarkets, cafés, cinemas and family attractions reflects the layered identity of modern Doha — part corporate capital, part regional shopping destination and part home to a large expatriate workforce.

Across the city, malls have developed distinct personalities. Some evoke European streets or grand architectural themes; others emphasize luxury boutiques, entertainment parks or neighborhood convenience. Together, they form a network of indoor social spaces connecting residents whose backgrounds span South Asia, Southeast Asia, the Middle East, Africa, Europe and the Americas.

On weekends, the crowds reveal that diversity. Families linger over long meals. Groups of friends move between coffee shops and cinemas. Domestic workers meet on their days off, while professionals shop for groceries after brunch. Teenagers circle the corridors in sneakers, occasionally spending more time socializing than shopping.

Arabic and English mix with Hindi, Urdu, Tagalog, Malayalam, French and other languages. The food courts can feel like condensed maps of migration, pairing global fast-food chains with biryani, shawarma, noodles and regional sweets.

## Consumption and connection

Qatar’s malls are also monuments to consumer culture.

Luxury watches, designer clothing and high-end cars speak to the country’s wealth, while familiar multinational brands offer expatriates a sense of continuity with places they have left behind. Seasonal promotions, product launches and elaborate displays turn shopping into spectacle.

But reducing Doha’s malls to temples of consumption misses their broader role.

In a city where many residents live far from extended family, malls offer accessible meeting points requiring little preparation. Visitors do not need an invitation, membership or special occasion. They can arrive alone and still become part of a crowd.

The appeal is especially strong for expatriates, who make up the majority of Qatar’s population. Their experience of the country can be temporary, shaped by work contracts and frequent departures. Against that transience, a regular café table, supermarket aisle or weekend mall visit can provide routine and familiarity.

The spaces are carefully managed and highly commercial, yet the social life inside them is often spontaneous. A quick shopping trip stretches into dinner. Children encounter school friends. Colleagues stop for coffee. A football performer draws strangers into a shared moment.

## A stage between the storefronts

Traore’s appearance at City Center demonstrated how malls increasingly function as cultural venues as well as retail destinations.

His freestyle routine required little translation. Each trick produced the same sequence across the audience: anticipation, surprise and applause. Football connected spectators who might otherwise have had little in common beyond being in the same building at the same time.

For travelers, Doha’s malls may not offer the historical atmosphere of Souq Waqif or the waterfront views of the Corniche. But they reveal another side of the capital — one rooted in migration, modernity and everyday habits.

Here, culture is not confined to museums or heritage sites. It unfolds over coffee, in food courts and beneath atrium lights, where a Guinean athlete can turn a shopping trip into a communal event.

In Doha, the mall is both marketplace and meeting place, a stage where the city’s global population comes indoors — and comes together.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.output:
**In Doha, the mall is more than a place to shop**

*Air-conditioned retail centers have become modern town squares in Qatar, where developers increasingly rely on spectacle—from freestyle football to indoor theme parks—to keep visitors coming.*

**DOHA** — A football rises above Iya Traore’s head, drops toward his shoulders and appears to stick to his body as he twists beneath it. Within moments, the Guinean freestyle soccer performer is balancing the ball on his neck, flicking it into the air and drawing a crowd of families and camera phones.

The show may have little to do with buying clothes or groceries. For the mall hosting it, that is precisely the point.

Across Doha, shopping centers compete not only through luxury brands and restaurant choices, but also through live performances, festivals, cinemas, play areas and other attractions designed to turn a retail trip into an outing. An appearance by an internationally known performer such as Traore—whose routines combine football technique, dance and acrobatics—can pull visitors into common areas, encourage them to stay longer and, developers hope, send them onward to shops and cafés.

In Qatar, that strategy builds on the unusually prominent role malls already play in daily life.

For much of the year, intense heat and humidity make outdoor gathering difficult, particularly during the day. Malls provide predictable comfort: air conditioning, shade, parking, security and access to food, prayer rooms and family facilities under one roof. They offer an indoor version of the public square, adapted to the Gulf climate.

On evenings and weekends, Doha’s largest malls fill with an array of visitors: Qatari families, young people meeting friends, expatriate workers, tourists and parents pushing strollers. Some arrive with shopping lists. Many come primarily to eat, walk or socialize.

That mix has made the mall one of the few spaces where the country’s diverse population regularly overlaps. Qatar’s residents come from across the Arab world, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Africa and Europe, and social networks can otherwise remain separated by language, occupation and income. A major shopping center, while still a commercial and managed environment, offers a shared destination.

Malls also fit the rhythms of family life. Restaurants provide easy meeting points for large groups, while cinemas, arcades and children’s zones allow different generations to spend several hours in the same building. During school holidays and festive periods, shopping centers often expand their programs with roaming characters, cultural displays, competitions and stage shows.

For developers, entertainment has become a way to distinguish one vast, polished complex from another.

Doha has added millions of square feet of retail space over the past two decades, including destination malls built around elaborate themes. Some feature canals or landscaped interiors; others offer ice rinks, amusement rides, snow attractions or performance spaces. The architecture itself is often presented as part of the experience.

This approach reflects a wider challenge facing physical retail. Online shopping can deliver products, but it cannot easily reproduce a family night out or the excitement of seeing a performer control a football at close range. Mall operators therefore sell time and experience as much as merchandise.

A freestyle soccer show is well suited to that model. It is visual, requires little translation and connects with Qatar’s enthusiasm for football, heightened by the country’s hosting of the 2022 FIFA World Cup. A routine can stop passersby almost instantly, while short clips circulate on social media and extend the mall’s publicity beyond the live audience.

The commercial logic is straightforward: a crowd around a performance creates energy, energy generates curiosity, and curiosity can increase footfall and the amount of time visitors spend inside. Nearby cafés may gain customers waiting for the show to begin; parents may combine it with dinner; children may persuade families to visit shops or attractions afterward.

Entertainment also helps malls shape their identities. A luxury-focused center may stage fashion or art events, while a family-oriented mall might emphasize cartoon characters, sports demonstrations or interactive games. During Ramadan and national celebrations, programming can shift toward heritage, crafts and community themes.

Yet the centrality of malls also reveals the limits of public life in a city built around cars and cooled interiors. Doha has invested in parks, promenades, cultural districts and the Metro, and its outdoor spaces become busy in the cooler months. Souq Waqif, the Corniche and newer pedestrian areas offer alternatives with a stronger sense of place.

Still, the mall remains dependable in every season. It asks little planning, accommodates mixed-age groups and combines practical errands with leisure.

As Traore keeps the ball aloft, the spectators form a temporary circle in a corridor designed to move consumers from one storefront to another. For a few minutes, the passage becomes a stadium and strangers become an audience.

That transformation—from shopping space to social stage—is why entertainment matters to Doha’s developers, and why malls have become so deeply embedded in Qatari life.

**Doha’s malls: Bluetooth flirtations, luxury labels and football magic**

*By a CNN correspondent in Doha*

In Doha, a shopping mall is rarely just a place to shop.

That became clear during an evening spent with Qatari friends, moving between gleaming storefronts, crowded cafés and polished marble corridors cooled to a temperature that made the desert outside feel like another country.

My friends treated the mall as both a meeting place and a stage. Families lingered over dinner, teenagers drifted between cinemas and coffee shops, and impeccably dressed shoppers examined watches and handbags whose price tags could rival the cost of a car.

Luxury was everywhere, but rarely loud. Men in crisp white thobes paused outside Italian boutiques. Women in flowing black abayas studied window displays bright with gold, silk and diamonds. Shopping bags from global fashion houses accumulated discreetly beneath café tables.

Yet beneath the mall’s orderly surface ran a quieter social current.

One of my companions explained how young people sometimes used Bluetooth to make contact across the traditional boundaries of public life. A phone’s discoverable name could become an invitation: a nickname, a joke or a short message sent to someone nearby. A glance across the atrium might confirm who was on the other end.

The exchange was cautious and coded—digital flirting conducted within a few meters, but with enough ambiguity for everyone to save face.

My friends laughed as they described the ritual: switch on Bluetooth, scan the nearby devices, guess which name belonged to which person and wait. Sometimes nothing happened. Sometimes a message appeared. Occasionally, a conversation continued long after both people had left the mall.

It felt like a distinctly local adaptation of technology—less like online dating than passing a note across a crowded room.

Then the crowd shifted.

In an open area near the shops, an African football performer had begun gathering an audience. With music playing, he balanced the ball on his forehead, rolled it around his neck and flicked it from one shoulder to the other. The ball seemed attached to him by an invisible thread.

Children pushed toward the front. Shoppers stopped mid-stride. Even the security guards appeared transfixed.

He spun the ball, trapped it behind his knee and sent it arcing over his head before catching it gently on the back of his neck. For a few minutes, the mall’s competing attractions—the boutiques, restaurants, phones and flirtations—fell away.

Doha is often described through its rapid transformation: the towers rising beside the Corniche, the luxury hotels, the ambitious architecture and the money that has remade the skyline. But an evening with friends in its shopping centers revealed something more intimate.

The mall was a climate-controlled town square: a place to see and be seen, to spend extravagantly or simply wander, to negotiate social customs and test new ones.

Outside, the night remained warm. Inside, beneath the bright lights, commerce, courtship and football had come together in one unlikely spectacle.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an observational article on Doha’s mall culture, contrasting it with American teenagers cruising malls and discussing how wealthy adult consumers socialize, shop, dine, and seek entertainment there.
counterfactuals.output:
## Doha After Dark: The Mall as a Modern Majlis

In the United States, the suburban mall is lodged in popular memory as teenage territory: a climate-controlled circuit where adolescents wandered without buying much, inspected one another’s clothes, shared fries, flirted near the fountain and stretched a modest allowance across an entire afternoon. “Cruising the mall” was less about commerce than independence. Before online shopping and smartphones weakened the mall’s social pull, it offered American teenagers a public place beyond the supervision of home and school.

In Doha, malls also function as social stages, but the leading actors are often affluent adults and families. On an evening or weekend, the city’s largest shopping centers fill not only with young people passing time but with professionals meeting friends, couples dining out, multigenerational families strolling and consumers treating retail as one part of a broader leisure ritual.

The setting matters. Doha’s heat makes air-conditioned interiors especially attractive for much of the year. Yet climate alone does not explain the mall’s importance. These complexes gather restaurants, cafés, cinemas, supermarkets, salons, children’s play areas and luxury boutiques in spaces that are polished, predictable and easy to navigate. Parking is plentiful, valet service is common, and the atmosphere is designed to make lingering feel legitimate.

By early evening, the mall begins to resemble a contemporary indoor promenade. Men in white thobes and women in black abayas move among expatriate residents dressed in business clothes, jeans, sportswear and designer fashion. Domestic workers accompany some families; children race toward entertainment zones; restaurant hosts manage queues. The crowd reflects Doha’s unusual social composition—Qatari citizens, long-term Arab residents, South Asian professionals, Western expatriates, tourists and service workers sharing a commercial environment, though not always sharing it in the same way.

Shopping is visible, but it is not necessarily the main event. A group of friends may spend more time over coffee than inside stores. A family might combine a supermarket trip with dinner and a film. A couple may browse watches, perfumes or handbags, then settle into a restaurant for the rest of the night. For wealthier consumers, shopping can become social performance: examining the newest collection, discussing a purchase with companions, recognizing acquaintances and displaying familiarity with global brands.

Luxury retail is central to this culture, but Doha’s malls sell more than expensive objects. They sell access to a global metropolitan lifestyle. Marble corridors, indoor canals, monumental chandeliers and meticulously composed storefronts place European fashion houses beside American restaurant chains and regional perfume brands. One mall may imitate an Italian streetscape; another may build its identity around scale, spectacle or architectural refinement. The point is not simply to provide shops but to create an environment worthy of an outing.

Dining is equally important. In the classic American teenage mall, the food court offered inexpensive fuel: pizza slices, pretzels, burgers and soft drinks consumed quickly. Doha’s malls retain food courts, but they also operate as restaurant districts. Tables fill with adults conducting informal business, friends extending an evening and families ordering elaborate meals. Coffee, in particular, provides a reason to remain in public without rushing. A cup can support an hour of conversation, people-watching or phone use.

Entertainment broadens the mall’s appeal further. Multiplex cinemas, bowling alleys, arcades, indoor amusement parks, ice rinks and elaborate children’s zones allow visitors to build an entire evening under one roof. Newer developments increasingly combine retail with hotels, landscaped outdoor areas and event spaces. During holidays and festivals, malls host performances, themed decorations and family activities, turning the commercial calendar into a civic one.

The comparison with American teenagers is revealing. Both cultures use the mall as a place to see and be seen. Both turn walking into a social activity and consumption into a language of belonging. But where the American mall cruiser traditionally sought temporary freedom from adults, Doha’s mall visitor often arrives as an adult exercising purchasing power. The outing may affirm family ties, professional status or cosmopolitan taste rather than adolescent autonomy.

That does not mean Doha’s malls are socially uniform. Teenagers still gather in groups, workers shop for necessities, and many visitors come for discounts rather than designer goods. Nor does everyone experience the mall’s luxury in the same way. The polished interior can bring sharply different incomes into close proximity while leaving the city’s hierarchies intact.

Still, the mall occupies an unusually broad place in Doha’s urban life. It is marketplace, dining room, playground, cinema, meeting hall and promenade. For affluent adults, it offers a public sphere organized around comfort, service and consumption—a modern majlis with storefronts, espresso machines and valet parking.

The American teenager cruised the mall because there was nowhere else to go. In Doha, wealthy adults often go because the mall has been designed to contain almost everywhere else.

# Mall Culture in Qatar: Where Tradition Meets Petro-Dollar Spectacle

In Qatar, shopping malls are more than places to buy clothes or escape the heat. They are air-conditioned town squares—part retail hub, part leisure park and part social stage. Fueled by decades of **petro-dollars**, the country’s mall culture reflects both rapid modernization and a distinctly Qatari appetite for family-oriented public life.

At **Landmark Shopping Center**, visitors move easily between international brands, cafés and entertainment venues. **City Center-Doha**, meanwhile, captures the larger-than-life side of the phenomenon: a vast commercial world where families can shop, dine, watch films in **movie theaters** and enjoy attractions that turn an ordinary outing into an all-day event. Across Qatar’s retail landscape, amenities such as indoor **skating rinks** underline how malls offer climate-controlled experiences that would be difficult to sustain outdoors for much of the year.

Yet Doha’s social life is not confined to polished shopping complexes. **Souq Waqif**, with its narrow lanes, spice stalls, restaurants and traditional architecture, provides a vivid counterpoint. Although it is not a modern mall, it serves a similar communal purpose—bringing residents and tourists together while linking contemporary Doha to the trading traditions of the Gulf.

The spectacle extends beyond shops and food courts. International performers have found enthusiastic audiences in Qatar, including **Guinean freestyle footballer Iya Traore**, whose acrobatic ball skills embody the energetic, cosmopolitan entertainment that increasingly accompanies the country’s public spaces and major events.

Qatar’s mall culture is therefore not simply about consumption. It is a product of wealth, climate, globalization and social custom—a world where luxury boutiques sit beside cinemas, skating attractions and family cafés, while the spirit of Souq Waqif remains close at hand.
